sanskrit.deva:
अथ हैनं सौर्यायणी गार्ग्यः पप्रच्छ ।
भगवन्नेतस्मिन्पुरुषे कानि स्वपन्ति ।
कान्यस्मिञ्जाग्रति ।
कतर एष देवः स्वप्नान्पश्यति ।
कस्यैतत्सुखं भवति ।
कस्मिन्नु सर्वे संप्रतिष्ठिता भवन्तीति ॥ १ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
atha hainaṃ sauryāyaṇī gārgyaḥ papraccha |
bhagavann etasmin puruṣe kāni svapanti |
kāny asmiñ jāgrati |
katara eṣa devaḥ svapnān paśyati |
kasyaitat sukhaṃ bhavati |
kasmin nu sarve saṃpratiṣṭhitā bhavantīti || 1 ||

padaccheda.iast: atha ha enam sauryāyaṇī gārgyaḥ papraccha bhagavan etasmin puruṣe kāni svapanti kāni asmin jāgrati kataraḥ eṣaḥ devaḥ svapnān paśyati kasya etat sukham bhavati kasmin nu sarve saṃpratiṣṭhitāḥ bhavanti iti
padaccheda.deva: अथ ह एनम् सौर्यायणी गार्ग्यः पप्रच्छ भगवन् एतस्मिन् पुरुषे कानि स्वपन्ति कानि अस्मिन् जाग्रति कतरः एषः देवः स्वप्नान् पश्यति कस्य एतत् सुखम् भवति कस्मिन् नु सर्वे संप्रतिष्ठिताः भवन्ति इति

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. pl.

translations.text: Then Sauryāyaṇin Gārgya asked him: ‘Venerable sir, which (organs) sleep in this person, and which stay awake in him? Which god is it that sees dreams? Whose is this happiness? And in what are all established together?’

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the praśna: with three questions all that falls within the lower knowledge has been completed: saṃsāra, whose field is the manifest, which consists of ends and means and is impermanent. Now that which is not end or means, without prāṇa, beyond the reach of mind and senses, auspicious, calm, changeless, imperishable, true, reached by the higher knowledge, called Puruṣa, within and without, unborn, has to be told: for this the next three questions are begun. The second Muṇḍaka says that, as sparks from a well-kindled fire, all beings are born from the supreme imperishable and merge in it again. What are those beings that are divided out of the imperishable? How, once divided, do they merge in it? What is the mark of that imperishable? Wishing to tell this, the text now raises the questions.

Śaṅkara: ‘in this person’, who has head, hands and the rest, which organs sleep, that is, cease from their own work, and which stay awake and do their own work? Which god, of those that are effects and those that are instruments, sees dreams? A dream is the seeing, inside the body and like waking, of one who has turned back from waking sight. When the work of waking and of dream has ceased, whose is the happiness that is serene, without effort, unobstructed? And at that time, in what are all, having ceased from the work of waking and dream, established together, become one, past telling apart, like the juices in honey or the rivers that have entered the sea?

Śaṅkara: it may be objected that organs which have ceased from their work, like sickles and other tools laid down, simply rest each in itself: whence the questioner's surmise that the organs of sleeping men go to oneness in something? The surmise is right. The organs are composite, serve the ends of an owner and are dependent in waking; so in sleep too it is reasonable that, being composite, they come together in something on which they depend. The question fits that surmise. It is asked by one who wishes to know the particular nature of that in which the aggregate of body and organs is dissolved in deep sleep and at the time of dissolution: who may that be?

sanskrit.deva:
तस्मै स होवाच ।
यथा गार्ग्य मरीचयोऽर्कस्यास्तं गच्छतः सर्वा एतस्मिंस्तेजोमण्डल एकीभवन्ति ।
ताः पुनः पुनरुदयतः प्रचरन्ति ।
एवं ह वै तत्सर्वं परे देवे मनस्येकीभवति ।
तेन तर्ह्येष पुरुषो न शृणोति ।
न पश्यति ।
न जिघ्रति ।
न रसयते ।
न स्पृशते ।
नाभिवदते ।
नादत्ते ।
नानन्दयते ।
न विसृजते ।
नेयायते ।
स्वपतीत्याचक्षते ॥ २ ॥

padaccheda.deva: तस्मै सः ह उवाच यथा गार्ग्य मरीचयः अर्कस्य अस्तम् गच्छतः सर्वाः एतस्मिन् तेजः-मण्डले एकी-भवन्ति ताः पुनः पुनः उदयतः प्रचरन्ति एवम् ह वै तत् सर्वम् परे देवे मनसि एकी-भवति तेन तर्हि एषः पुरुषः न शृणोति न पश्यति न जिघ्रति न रसयते न स्पृशते न अभिवदते न आदत्ते न आनन्दयते न विसृजते न इयायते स्वपति इति आचक्षते

translations.text: He said to him: ‘As, O Gārgya, all the rays of the setting sun become one in that orb of light, and go forth again when it rises again, so all that becomes one in the higher god, the mind. Therefore at that time this person does not hear, see, smell, taste or touch, does not speak, grasp, enjoy, discharge or move about. They say: he sleeps.’

notes: Śaṅkara: as all the rays of the sun when it goes to setting, out of sight, become one in that orb, a mass of light, past telling apart, and are spread abroad again when that same sun rises, so all that, the objects, the senses and the rest, becomes one, at the time of dream, in the mind, which is the higher god because the eye and the other gods depend on it; and when the person is about to wake they go forth from the mind to their own work, like the rays from the orb. Since at the time of sleep the ear and the other organs by which sound and the rest are perceived are as if one in the mind and have ceased from their work, the person, Devadatta or another, does not hear and so on; people say ‘he sleeps’.
The mūla reads svapatīty; the bhāṣya has svapiti.

sanskrit.deva:
प्राणाग्नय एवैतस्मिन्पुरे जाग्रति ।
गार्हपत्यो ह वा एषोऽपानः ।
व्यानोऽन्वाहार्यपचनः ।
यद्गार्हपत्यात्प्रणीयते प्रणयनात् ।
आहवनीयः प्राणः ॥ ३ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
prāṇāgnaya evaitasmin pure jāgrati |
gārhapatyo ha vā eṣo 'pānaḥ |
vyāno 'nvāhāryapacanaḥ |
yad gārhapatyāt praṇīyate praṇayanāt |
āhavanīyaḥ prāṇaḥ || 3 ||

padaccheda.iast: prāṇa-agnayaḥ eva etasmin pure jāgrati gārhapatyaḥ ha vai eṣaḥ apānaḥ vyānaḥ anvāhāryapacanaḥ yat gārhapatyāt praṇīyate praṇayanāt āhavanīyaḥ prāṇaḥ
padaccheda.deva: प्राण-अग्नयः एव एतस्मिन् पुरे जाग्रति गार्हपत्यः ह वै एषः अपानः व्यानः अन्वाहार्यपचनः यत् गार्हपत्यात् प्रणीयते प्रणयनात् आहवनीयः प्राणः

words.meaning: the fires that are the breaths
from that from which it is taken

translations.text: The fires of the breaths alone stay awake in this city (the body). This apāna is the gārhapatya fire; the vyāna is the southern fire; and prāṇa is the āhavanīya fire, because it is taken forth from the gārhapatya, from which that fire is taken.

notes: Śaṅkara: when the ear and the other organs sleep, in this city, the body with its nine gates, the five airs, prāṇa and the rest, stay awake like fires. The text states their likeness to the fires. The apāna is the gārhapatya: for at the time of the agnihotra the other fire, the āhavanīya, is taken forth from the gārhapatya, which is the praṇayana, that from which it is taken; so in one who sleeps prāṇa is as it were taken forth from the working of the apāna and moves through the mouth and the nose, and therefore stands in the place of the āhavanīya. The vyāna goes out from the heart by the southern opening, and from this connection with the south it is the anvāhāryapacana, the southern fire.

sanskrit.deva:
यदुच्छ्वासनिःश्वासावेतावाहुती समं नयतीति स समानः ।
मनो ह वाव यजमानः ।
इष्टफलमेवोदानः ।
स एनं यजमानमहरहर्ब्रह्म गमयति ॥ ४ ॥

mano ha vāva yajamānaḥ |
iṣṭaphalam evodānaḥ |
sa enaṃ yajamānam aharahar brahma gamayati || 4 ||

lines.iast: yad ucchvāsaniḥśvāsāv etāv āhutī samaṃ nayatīti sa samānaḥ
sa enaṃ yajamānam aharahar brahma gamayati

padaccheda.iast: yat ucchvāsa-niḥśvāsau etau āhutī samam nayati iti saḥ samānaḥ manaḥ ha vāva yajamānaḥ iṣṭa-phalam eva udānaḥ saḥ enam yajamānam ahar-ahar brahma gamayati
padaccheda.deva: यत् उच्छ्वास-निःश्वासौ एतौ आहुती समम् नयति इति सः समानः मनः ह वाव यजमानः इष्ट-फलम् एव उदानः सः एनम् यजमानम् अहर्-अहर् ब्रह्म गमयति

translations.text: Because it carries evenly these two oblations, the in-breath and the out-breath, it is the samāna (the hotṛ). The mind is the sacrificer. The udāna is the fruit of the sacrifice: day after day it leads this sacrificer to Brahman.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: and here the hotṛ of the agnihotra is this.

Śaṅkara: the in-breath and the out-breath are like the two oblations of the agnihotra, being always two. The air that carries them evenly, so that the body may last, though it stands in the place of a fire, is the hotṛ, because it carries the oblations: that is the samāna. So even the sleep of one who knows is the offering of the agnihotra, and the meaning is that one who knows should not be thought to be without rites; for the Vājasaneyaka says that all beings at all times pile the fires for him even while he sleeps.

Śaṅkara: here, with the fires of the breaths awake, the mind, having withdrawn the outer organs and the objects, and wishing to go to Brahman as to heaven, the fruit of the agnihotra, stays awake as the sacrificer: it is imagined as the sacrificer because, like him, it is the chief in the dealings of body and organs, and because it has set out towards Brahman as he towards heaven. The air udāna is the fruit of the sacrifice, since the fruit is reached by means of the udāna: it makes the sacrificer called mind fall even from its state of dream and day after day, at the time of deep sleep, leads it to Brahman, the imperishable, as to heaven.

Śaṅkara, going on: thus for one who knows, from the time the ear and the rest cease until he rises from sleep, there is only the experience of the fruit of all sacrifices, and it is not for his harm, as it is for those who do not know: so knowing is praised. For it is not only in one who knows that the ear and the rest sleep, or the fires of the breaths stay awake, or the mind, free in waking and dream, goes day by day to deep sleep; the passing in turn through waking, dream and deep sleep is common to all living things. So this can only be praise of knowing. What was asked, ‘which god sees dreams’, is now answered.
The e-text reads mano ha vāvana yajamānaḥ; it is set right here to vāva, as the bhāṣya has it.

sanskrit.deva:

देशदिगन्तरैश्च प्रत्यनुभूतं पुनः पुनः प्रत्यनुभवति ।
दृष्टं चादृष्टं च श्रुतं चाश्रुतं चानुभूतं चाननुभूतं च सच्चासच्च सर्वं पश्यति ।
सर्वः पश्यति ॥ ५ ॥

translations.text: Here, in dream, this god (the mind) experiences his greatness. What he has seen he sees again as seen; what he has heard he hears again as heard; what he has experienced in other places and quarters he experiences again and again. The seen and the unseen, the heard and the unheard, the experienced and the unexperienced, the real and the unreal: he sees all, and being all he sees.

notes: Śaṅkara: here, when the ear and the rest have ceased and the airs, prāṇa and the others, are awake to guard the body, in the interval before deep sleep is reached, this god, who has drawn the ear and the other organs into himself as the sun its rays, experiences in dream his greatness, his becoming many as subject and as object.

Śaṅkara: an objection: in experiencing this greatness the mind is the instrument of the experiencer; how can it be said to experience it of itself? It is the knower of the field that is independent. The answer: there is no fault. The independence of the knower of the field is itself made by the adjunct, mind; in truth he neither sleeps nor wakes of himself. His waking and his dream are made by the adjunct, mind, as the Vājasaneyaka says: ‘becoming dream, he thinks as it were, he moves as it were’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.7). So it is right to speak of the mind as independent in experiencing this greatness.

Śaṅkara: some say that if at the time of dream the knower of the field has the mind as adjunct, his being his own light is contradicted. Not so: their error comes from not knowing the sense of scripture. All talk of being one's own light and the like, up to liberation, lies within ignorance and is produced by the adjuncts, mind and the rest: ‘where there is as it were another, there one may see another’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.31), ‘there is contact with the elements’, ‘but where all has become the Self alone, by what should one see whom?’ (2.4.14). So this is a doubt of those who know Brahman dimly, not of those who know the one Self.

Śaṅkara: but then the qualification ‘here this Puruṣa is his own light’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.9) would have no purpose. The reply: that is saying too little. By ‘he lies in the space within the heart’ (2.1.17), which bounds him within the heart, his being his own light would be contradicted all the more. ‘Granted that this fault may be; still in dream, by his being his own light alone, half the burden is taken off.’ No: there too scripture says ‘he lies in the purītat’ (2.1.19), so there is a connection with the channels of the purītat, and the idea of taking off half the burden is false. How then ‘here this Puruṣa is his own light’? If it is said that that scripture, being of another branch, need not be regarded: no, for one sense is accepted; the one Self is the sense of all the Vedāntas, what they mean to teach and what is to be known. So it is right to show how the Self's being its own light in dream is possible, since scripture reveals the truth as it is.

Śaṅkara: then hear the sense of scripture, giving up all conceit; by conceit it cannot be known in a hundred years by all those who think themselves learned. As one who sleeps in the space of the heart, in the purītat and in the channels has no connection with them and can be shown apart from them, so that the Self's being its own light is not contradicted, so too here: in the mind, which holds the impressions that have arisen from ignorance, desire and action, the seer, wholly apart from all effects and instruments, sees through ignorance the impressions caused by action as if they were other things; and because he is other than the impressions, which are what is seen, his being his own light cannot be denied even by the proudest logician. So it is well said that, when the organs are merged in the mind and the mind is not merged, he, made of mind, sees dreams.

Śaṅkara: how does he experience greatness? A friend or a son seen before: scented by that impression, he thinks, through ignorance, that he sees the son or friend who has arisen from the impression; so too he hears as it were, and experiences again as it were what was experienced in other places and quarters. ‘Seen’: in this birth; ‘unseen’: seen in another birth, for there can be no impression of what was never seen at all. So with the heard and the unheard. ‘Experienced’: in this birth, by the mind alone; ‘unexperienced’: experienced by the mind in another birth. The real is real water and the like; the unreal is the water of a mirage and the like. In short he sees all, and being all he sees: with all the impressions of the mind as his adjunct, the god mind, the self of all the organs, sees dreams.
The e-text reads yad dṛṣṭaṃ iṣṭam; it is set right here to dṛṣṭaṃ dṛṣṭam, as the bhāṣya takes it.

padaccheda.deva: सः यदा तेजसा अभिभूतः भवति अत्र एषः देवः स्वप्नान् न पश्यति अथ तदा एतस्मिन् शरीरे एतत् सुखम् भवति

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: When he is overcome by light, then this god sees no dreams; and then this happiness arises in this body.

notes: Śaṅkara: when the god in the form of mind is overcome on every side by the sun's light called bile, which lies in the channels, the door of the impressions is shut, and the rays of the mind, together with the organs, are drawn into the heart. When the mind stays pervading the whole body in the form of consciousness without distinctions, like fire in wood, then he is in deep sleep. At that time the god called mind sees no dreams, the door of seeing being closed by the light. Then this happiness arises in the body: consciousness that is unobstructed, pervades the body without distinction and is serene.

Śaṅkara, going on to the next mantra: at this time the body and the organs, which are bound to ignorance, desire and action, are stilled. When they are stilled, the Self's own nature, which the adjuncts make appear otherwise, is without a second, one, auspicious, calm. To show this very state by the entering in of earth and the rest, down to their subtle forms, which ignorance has made, the text gives an example.

sanskrit.deva:
स यथा सोम्य वयांसि वासोवृक्षं संप्रतिष्ठन्ते ।
एवं ह वै तत्सर्वं पर आत्मनि संप्रतिष्ठते ॥ ७ ॥

padaccheda.deva: सः यथा सोम्य वयांसि वासः-वृक्षम् संप्रतिष्ठन्ते एवम् ह वै तत् सर्वम् परे आत्मनि संप्रतिष्ठते

words.meaning: to the tree where they dwell

translations.text: As birds, dear one, resort to the tree where they dwell, so all that comes to rest in the supreme Self.

notes: Śaṅkara: saḥ: this is the example. somya: you who are pleasant to look upon. As birds go to the tree that is their dwelling, so all that is about to be named comes to rest in the supreme Self, the imperishable. What is ‘all that’?

words.meaning: what is to be taken as ‘I’
what one is to be aware of
what is to be lit up

translations.text: Earth and the subtle element of earth, water and its subtle element, fire and its subtle element, air and its subtle element, space and its subtle element; the eye and what is to be seen, the ear and what is to be heard, the nose and what is to be smelt, taste and what is to be tasted, the skin and what is to be touched; speech and what is to be spoken, the hands and what is to be grasped, the organ of generation and what is to be enjoyed, the anus and what is to be discharged, the feet and what is to be walked; the mind and what is to be thought, the understanding and what is to be understood, the sense of ‘I’ and what is to be taken as ‘I’, awareness and what one is to be aware of, lustre and what is to be lit up, prāṇa and what is to be upheld.

notes: Śaṅkara: earth is the gross element with its five qualities; the earth-mātrā is its cause, the subtle element of smell; so with water, fire, air and space: the meaning is the gross and the subtle elements. Then the organs of knowledge and of action, each with its object. The mind, named before, and its object; the understanding, whose nature is determination, and its object; the sense of ‘I’, the inner organ marked by self-regard, and its object; citta, the inner organ that has awareness, and its object. tejas: the skin that has lustre, as distinct from the organ of touch; what is to be lit up is the object it makes shine. prāṇa: what they call the thread; what is to be upheld is all that it strings together. For the whole mass of effects and instruments, composite and existing for the sake of another, made of name and form, is just this much.
Śaṅkara, going on to the next mantra: beyond this is that form of the Self which has entered here as enjoyer and doer, like the sun in water.

sanskrit.deva:
एष हि द्रष्टा स्प्रष्टा श्रोता घ्राता रसयिता मन्ता बोद्धा कर्ता विज्ञानात्मा पुरुषः ।
स परेऽक्षर आत्मनि संप्रतिष्ठते ॥ ९ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
eṣa hi draṣṭā spraṣṭā śrotā ghrātā rasayitā mantā boddhā kartā vijñānātmā puruṣaḥ |
sa pare 'kṣara ātmani saṃpratiṣṭhate || 9 ||

lines.iast: eṣa hi draṣṭā spraṣṭā śrotā ghrātā rasayitā mantā boddhā kartā vijñānātmā puruṣaḥ
lines.deva: एष हि द्रष्टा स्प्रष्टा श्रोता घ्राता रसयिता मन्ता बोद्धा कर्ता विज्ञानात्मा पुरुषः

padaccheda.iast: eṣaḥ hi draṣṭā spraṣṭā śrotā ghrātā rasayitā mantā boddhā kartā vijñāna-ātmā puruṣaḥ saḥ pare akṣare ātmani saṃpratiṣṭhate
padaccheda.deva: एषः हि द्रष्टा स्प्रष्टा श्रोता घ्राता रसयिता मन्ता बोद्धा कर्ता विज्ञान-आत्मा पुरुषः सः परे अक्षरे आत्मनि संप्रतिष्ठते

translations.text: This is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the one who understands, the doer, the Puruṣa whose nature is knowing. He comes to rest in the supreme imperishable Self.

notes: Śaṅkara: vijñāna as ‘that by which one knows’ is an instrument, the understanding and the like; here it is ‘that which knows’, the agent: he has that for his self, his nature, that is, he has the nature of a knower. He is Puruṣa because he fills the adjunct that has been described, the aggregate of body and organs. As the reflection of the sun in water enters the sun, so he comes to rest in the supreme imperishable Self, which remains as the support of the world.
Śaṅkara, going on to the next mantra: the text states the fruit for one who knows that oneness.

sanskrit.deva:
परमेवाक्षरं प्रतिपद्यते ।
स यो ह वै तदच्छायमशरीरमलोहितं शुभ्रमक्षरं वेदयते यस्तु सोम्य ।
स सर्वज्ञः सर्वो भवति ।
तदेष श्लोकः ॥ १० ॥
sanskrit.iast:
param evākṣaraṃ pratipadyate |
sa yo ha vai tadacchāyam aśarīram alohitaṃ śubhram akṣaraṃ vedayate yas tu somya |
sa sarvajñaḥ sarvo bhavati |
tad eṣa ślokaḥ || 10 ||

lines.iast: sa yo ha vai tadacchāyam aśarīram alohitaṃ śubhram akṣaraṃ vedayate yas tu somya
lines.deva: स यो ह वै तदच्छायमशरीरमलोहितं शुभ्रमक्षरं वेदयते यस्तु सोम्य

padaccheda.iast: param eva akṣaram pratipadyate saḥ yaḥ ha vai tat acchāyam aśarīram alohitam śubhram akṣaram vedayate yaḥ tu somya saḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvaḥ bhavati tat eṣaḥ ślokaḥ
padaccheda.deva: परम् एव अक्षरम् प्रतिपद्यते सः यः ह वै तत् अच्छायम् अशरीरम् अलोहितम् शुभ्रम् अक्षरम् वेदयते यः तु सोम्य सः सर्वज्ञः सर्वः भवति तत् एषः श्लोकः

translations.text: He attains the supreme imperishable itself who knows that imperishable, without shadow, without body, without colour, pure. He, dear one, becomes all-knowing, becomes all. On this there is this verse:

notes: Śaṅkara: he who, freed from all desires, knows that: acchāyam, free of darkness; aśarīram, free of the body that is all the adjuncts of name and form; alohitam, free of red and all other qualities; and for that reason śubhram, pure; akṣaram, because it is without any qualification; true, called Puruṣa, without prāṇa, beyond the reach of mind, auspicious, calm, within and without, unborn. He who knows it, having given up everything, is all-knowing: nothing can be unknown to him. Before, through ignorance, he was not all-knowing; when ignorance is removed by knowledge he becomes all.
The e-text reads sa sarvaḥ sarvo bhavati; it is set right here to sa sarvajñaḥ, as the bhāṣya has it.

sanskrit.deva:
विज्ञानात्मा सह देवैश्च सर्वैः प्राणा भूतानि संप्रतिष्ठन्ति यत्र ।
तदक्षरं वेदयते यस्तु सोम्य स सर्वज्ञः सर्वमेवाविवेशेति ॥ ११ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
vijñānātmā saha devaiś ca sarvaiḥ prāṇā bhūtāni saṃpratiṣṭhanti yatra |
tad akṣaraṃ vedayate yas tu somya sa sarvajñaḥ sarvam evāviveśeti || 11 ||

lines.iast: vijñānātmā saha devaiś ca sarvaiḥ prāṇā bhūtāni saṃpratiṣṭhanti yatra
lines.deva: विज्ञानात्मा सह देवैश्च सर्वैः प्राणा भूतानि संप्रतिष्ठन्ति यत्र

lines.iast: tad akṣaraṃ vedayate yas tu somya sa sarvajñaḥ sarvam evāviveśeti
lines.deva: तदक्षरं वेदयते यस्तु सोम्य स सर्वज्ञः सर्वमेवाविवेशेति

padaccheda.iast: vijñāna-ātmā saha devaiḥ ca sarvaiḥ prāṇāḥ bhūtāni saṃpratiṣṭhanti yatra tat akṣaram vedayate yaḥ tu somya saḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvam eva āviveśa iti
padaccheda.deva: विज्ञान-आत्मा सह देवैः च सर्वैः प्राणाः भूतानि संप्रतिष्ठन्ति यत्र तत् अक्षरम् वेदयते यः तु सोम्य सः सर्वज्ञः सर्वम् एव आविवेश इति

words.meaning: the self whose nature is knowing

translations.text: He who knows that imperishable in which the self whose nature is knowing, with all the gods, the breaths and the elements, comes to rest: he, dear one, is all-knowing and enters into all.

notes: Śaṅkara: the gods are Agni and the rest; the breaths are the eye and the rest; the elements are earth and the rest. āviveśa: enters.
